A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FedMosaic, PQ-LoRA, and DRAKE despite the revised title and SIMA-to-RELA renaming. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, adaptation experiments, client-level results, and ablations on DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Aya, and its named Fed-LLM setup.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds cross-family evaluations, Fed-LLM-Large experiments, and extensive sensitivity and robustness analyses.

M1.justification: RELA retains SIMA's EMA-gradient-based similarity weighting but adds Gaussian noise and random coordinate subsampling to the gradient pipeline (Section 4.1 and Algorithm 1). This changes the information transmitted and used for aggregation. PQ-LoRA's architecture and block-wise alignment approach remain substantially intact.

E1.justification: V2 adds Fed-LLM-Large, combining instruction-following data from Fed-ChatbotIT, Fed-Aya, and Fed-FLAN, and uses ChatbotIT and VisualStorytelling in alignment-data experiments. DRAKE's tasks remain unchanged. Fed-Scope matches the earlier five-client general-capability, mathematics, and coding coverage; its new name alone does not establish added coverage.

E2.justification: The main FL comparator roster remains. V2 adds an adapted NBS comparator in Table 33, adds FedSim, TAKFL, and FedDAT to the corresponding five-client text evaluation, and replaces PerAda with FedDAT in the Fed-Aya comparison (v1 Tables 4 and 14; v2 Table 20). Other newly discussed methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 52-client Fed-LLM-Large protocol with two tasks per client, four communication rounds, ten local steps, and ROUGE-L evaluation (Section A.6). It also adds mixed Llama/Qwen configurations, randomized client-model assignments, fixed-budget communication/local-step comparisons, and auxiliary-model quantization settings.

E4.justification: V1's rank, block-count, gradient-source, and alignment ablations are retained. V2 substantially extends analysis to public-data size and domain mismatch, randomized model assignment, temperature, EMA, noise and compression sensitivity, lighter auxiliary models, and computational and communication scaling. The main component ablation replaces HFLB with Fed-Scope.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds and report means with standard deviations in Section 6.1. V2 extends this reporting practice to additional experiments without introducing new confidence intervals, significance tests, or an increased run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds cross-family, 52-client, and extensive sensitivity results. Existing entries also change: FedMosaic's DRAKE-Static Self AAUC changes from 64.24 to 64.64, and HFLB-Dynamic Self Alast from 80.90 to 80.80. The heterogeneous HFLB-Static comparison is removed. Many original DRAKE-Dynamic and appendix results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorems 1 and 2 and their proofs are retained. Section 4.2.2 specifies rectangular CCA projections and replaces the ordinary inverse with an explicit pseudoinverse in the back-projection formula, a limited mathematical correction. The appendix still retains the older inverse formula.

C1.justification: The three central contributions and claims of improved personalization, generalization, and adaptation remain. V2's abstract strengthens the privacy assertion to collaboration 'without privacy risks,' beyond v1's statement that collaboration avoids sharing data. The title and SIMA-to-RELA renaming otherwise preserve the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of public-data robustness, privacy–accuracy tradeoffs, communication frequency, model assignment, and NBS's weaker personalization. V1's ten-client limitation is replaced by limitations concerning untested speech/time-series modalities and broader architectures (v1 Section A.19; v2 Section A.26).

D1.justification: V2 supplies previously missing alignment details: LLaVA-Instruct-158K, 5,000 examples, one epoch, batch size four, Adam, a cosine scheduler, and learning rate 5e-5 (Section A.17). It also adds consolidated model configurations and EMA/sanitization defaults. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation; code release remains promised rather than established.

R1.justification: New Sections A.22 and A.25 substantially expand positioning against similarity-aware FL, multi-task learning, and alternative multimodal benchmarks. They distinguish RELA from pFedSim, pFedHR, Flashback, FEDLAW, NBS, and RotoGrad, alongside new privacy references and benchmark comparisons. This exceeds the accompanying citation-style changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively rewritten around collaborative personalization. SIMA becomes RELA, preliminary material is condensed, and appendix analyses are reorganized. The NeurIPS checklist is removed, while ICLR ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are introduced.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to show the sanitization pipeline, a CKA example is redisplayed in the main text, and new cost and sensitivity plots are added. Main results and model-validation tables are split or regrouped, with substantial caption and layout changes. Many original appendix graphics are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central heterogeneous-collaboration claim through mixed-family experiments, a 52-client evaluation, and public-data mismatch and randomized-assignment tests absent from v1. These address important validation gaps, while the alignment recipe improves reproducibility. The gains outweigh the omitted heterogeneous HFLB-Static comparison. However, stronger privacy claims remain unvalidated, and Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 disagree about whether noise precedes or follows EMA.
